opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. People often look at my papers and see a bit of a scattered picture: some work on grokking, some on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, some on physics-inspired generative models, some on interpretability, some on AI for science. From the outside it can look like I'm jumping around. From the inside, it feels like one question approached from different angles.

The way I'd put it is that I'm a physicist by training, and I care about **understanding**. That cuts in two directions. One direction is "AI for science": can we build tools that help us understand nature, discover laws, find symbolic formulas, make models that scientists can actually read and reason with? The other direction is "science of AI": can we treat neural networks themselves as physical systems and understand them the way a physicist understands a gas or a crystal? Why do they suddenly generalize, like in grokking? What structures form inside them? What are the phase transitions?

These two directions feed each other. When I study how networks learn, I get ideas for designing more interpretable architectures. KAN came partly from that: if we want AI to help with science, the model should be something you can open up and see the formula inside. And when I try to use AI for physics problems, I run into failures that force me to ask basic questions about how these models represent things.

So the variety is real at the level of topics, but the underlying motivation is quite consistent. I think of it as a loop: physics helps us understand AI, and AI helps us understand physics. And I've found that if you only stay in one narrow subfield, you miss a lot of the connections. Some of my favorite ideas came from taking a concept from one area, say a toy model from statistical physics, and asking, "What does this look like in a neural network?"

I'll also admit there's a personal element. I get bored easily. I like the stage of research where things are still messy and nobody knows the right questions yet. Once a field becomes very mature and it's mostly about pushing benchmarks by half a percent, I tend to drift toward something newer. That's maybe a strength and a weakness at the same time. But I'd like to think the thread of curiosity, of wanting to really understand rather than just make things work, holds it all together.

r001.rationale: The response describes a unifying motivation across his interests, but does not say that Liu recognized this thread retrospectively.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. People look at my work and see a scattered list: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, grokking, AI for physics, mechanistic interpretability, a bit of neuroscience. From the outside it looks like I can't sit still. From the inside, it feels like one question asked from different directions.

The question is roughly this: what is the relationship between intelligence and structure? Physics taught me to believe that behind messy phenomena there are usually simple laws, and that finding the right representation is most of the work. When I look at a neural network, I am asking the same thing I would ask about a gas or a magnet. What are the few variables that actually matter? What is the phase diagram? Grokking is interesting to me not as a training curiosity but because it looks like a phase transition, with memorization and generalization as two different phases. KANs came from the opposite side: if we care about structure and interpretability, why not build it into the architecture from the start, so that the model speaks a language a scientist can read?

So I would say the variety is in the objects, not in the motivation. Sometimes I study networks to understand them as physical systems. Sometimes I use physics intuition to design networks. Sometimes I use networks to rediscover physics. Those feel like three faces of the same project, which is to make the connection between science and AI run in both directions.

There is also an honest personal answer, which is that I get bored, and I find that a new angle often unblocks an old problem. Physicists have a tradition of being tourists in other fields. I try to be a respectful tourist, but I do believe that carrying a few tools across borders is where many of the interesting things happen.

r001.rationale: The response describes a unifying question behind his research, but does not say he recognized that thread retrospectively or indicate that this understanding came later.

astra-6.text:
I think the variety is more apparent than real. In my mind, these interests are connected by a question: how can we find simple, understandable principles behind complicated systems? In physics, you’re looking for patterns that explain many observations. With machine learning, I’m interested in whether we can discover those patterns from data—and whether we can understand what the model has learned.

So I don’t necessarily start by saying, “I want to work in this field.” I get curious about a question, and then I follow it, even if that means learning tools from another field. From the outside, that can look like switching interests. From the inside, it feels like following the same thread.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies a unifying question behind the research interests, but does not say this connection was recognized retrospectively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the variety is more apparent than real. For me, there’s a common question underneath: how can we understand something complicated through a few simple principles? Physics asks that about nature, and machine learning gives us another setting in which to explore it.

Sometimes I’m interested in using AI to help discover scientific structure, and sometimes I’m interested in understanding the structure of AI itself. Those can look like different directions, but to me they’re closely connected. In both cases, I want to go beyond getting a result and ask why it works, what the essential ingredients are, and whether we can express that understanding simply.

r001.rationale: He identifies a common question beneath his varied interests, but does not say he recognized that unifying thread retrospectively or arrived at it after the fact.
